title: Greeks and Delta Hedging: Naked Positions, Stop-Loss Trading, Dynamic Rebalancing, and Gamma Risk
prerequisites: Black-Scholes-Merton European option pricing formulas and normal distribution
Option Delta definition and sensitivity to underlying asset prices
Interest rate compounding and present value discounting
learningOutcomes: Evaluate the risks of naked option writing, covered stock positions, and stop-loss trading leakage ([fact-01], [fact-02]).
Calculate option Delta for calls, puts, and dividend-paying assets ([fact-03]).
Construct and dynamically rebalance delta-neutral portfolios for institutional option writing ([fact-04], [fact-05]).
Analyze rebalancing friction, transaction costs, and tolerance bands in real-world trading ([fact-06]).
Define the major Greeks (Delta, Gamma, Theta, Vega, Rho) and use second-order Taylor series approximations to manage Gamma risk ([fact-07], [fact-08], [fact-09]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Stop-loss strategies suffer from severe transaction costs and guaranteed cash leakage because volatile markets cause frequent whipsaws around the strike price, forcing traders to repeatedly buy high and sell low ([fact-02]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: In a BSM arbitrage-free market, the expected cumulative cost of dynamic delta hedging exactly equals the upfront option premium received; delta hedging transforms risk into rebalancing and transaction friction rather than free alpha ([fact-10]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Delta is a linear approximation valid only for infinitesimal price moves. Large discrete jumps change Delta itself due to Gamma curvature, creating non-linear P&L drift that requires Gamma management ([fact-08], [fact-09]).

activeRecallQuiz.scenario: A financial institution writes 100,000 European call options with K = $50, S0 = $49, r = 5%, sigma = 20%, and T = 20 weeks. The initial option delta is 0.522, requiring the bank to buy 52,200 shares at $49 ($2,557,800). By week 1, the stock drops to $48.12, and delta drops to 0.458.
activeRecallQuiz.question: 1) How many shares must the bank buy or sell at week 1 to restore delta neutrality? 2) Why does dynamic delta hedging fail to generate risk-free alpha?
activeRecallQuiz.correctAnswer: Correctly identifying the downside risk and margin constraints.
activeRecallQuiz.explanation: Detailed pedagogical explanation grounded in source principles.

coreTakeaways: Naive hedging strategies like naked writing and stop-loss trading expose institutions to catastrophic losses and severe rebalancing leakage ([fact-01], [fact-02]).
Dynamic delta neutrality requires continuously adjusting share holdings ($Q \cdot \Delta$) as asset prices and time evolve ([fact-04], [fact-05]).
Delta hedging is a linear approximation that leaves portfolios exposed to non-linear Gamma curvature, requiring second-order risk management and tolerance bands ([fact-06], [fact-08], [fact-09]).
